lines.text: No judging — that's the way it should be. It's DVDASA. Sometimes I like to say it — David Choe. And thank you to Head of Security, Critter, for keeping us all safe. No judging. No judging.

No judging. No judging. Welcome one, welcome all. It's DVDASA, with your host David Choe, and your co-host Critter. Here we go — special edition. So we... it was all-you-can-eat. We just came back from the game.

There was hot dogs and shit. — All you could eat what? Everything? — Everything. Oh, here's our friends, come in. We've got to answer one serious question. — Absolutely, player. We just came back from a Dodgers game.
Yes. And — oh yeah, if you guys want to wear these. We just came back from a Dodgers game. I just met Dave at his birthday, which he invited me to — because you inspired me to throw it there.
Dave's from L.A. — I've heard about this. It was a badass birthday party. He did graffiti growing up in a crew called KGB. — Yes, sir. Kids Gone Bad. Which is different than my crew.
My crew was me and Harry — Koreans Gone Bad. Dave's was Kids Gone Bad, or Killer Green Buds, or whatever. — No, Killer Green Buds was second. Okay, I'll tell you a story about Killer Green Buds.
They rolled up about ten years late. We started our shit in like '82, literally. And then, like, ten years later — did you battle, like a fight battle, or graffiti? — No, we did a graffiti battle.

Okay, so the story goes: somebody shows up trying to say they're KGB — after we've been doing this shit since, like, '81, '82. Seriously. I threw a tag on the side of an RTD bus before I'd ever seen people tagging on RTD buses.
Right. We saw, like, 18th Street, MS, all the gangster shit. But they weren't doing buses, for some reason. Our friend had an artistic mom — she took us to see Wild Style.

Blew our minds — but in an art theater. So we were ahead of our time in the L.A.-to-New-York transition of graffiti. When we first started tagging it was like, fuck — I literally wrote on the side of the bus and had never seen it done before.
So it was like, boom — we were early in the L.A. shit, you know what I mean? So then, ten years later, some kids are like... Now, this is the thing I see now.
We're old now. I don't have— — Oh, come on. Come on. Speak for yourself. — No, listen. We were kids doing graffiti. And now a lot of these kids have families. They're married. They have children.
Absolutely. And most of them went on. There's still some late-30, 40-year-olds still writing — on your feet — like David Choe. — I respect it. — I can't get caught myself. I mean, it's crazy.

I can't get caught myself. It's a sickness. It's a sickness — they can't stop. They have real responsibilities now. They have children, they have family. They could go to jail. It's not like you're a teenager.
Well, you know Robbie Conal. — Yeah. He was, like, the baddest. When we were out there on the streets doing the shit — we're fucking tagging, we're doing all this shit.

And we start seeing these fucking posters — 'It Can't Happen Here,' and 'Contra Diction.' [reading them off] Contra Diction. The Ronald Reagan thing — when Reagan was president, he was putting up these posters that said 'Contra Diction.'
Right. And I was like, fuck, what's this? What's he doing? This is one of the first artists doing shit like that. And we were tagging around, running around.
We were down by Alvarado, by MacArthur Park. And Otis Parsons was there — they had a show. We just stumbled onto it, as little kids.
Radiotron used to be down there too, right by Otis Parsons. We stumble in midday, into some art show — and it's Robbie Conal's fucking paintings.
And they're big. And they're not posters anymore — they're thick. Thick, like Chris Rock. — Yes, and they've got fucking combs going through the hair. — Yeah. And I'm like, oh shit.
It gave me a fucking brain meltdown of art. Like, oh shit — there's something deeper going on here. — Hell yes. — But Dave, talking about art is beyond the most boring shit ever.

Yeah. We have to get to the bottom of a very serious question. — Absolutely. Okay — you have a big family. — Uh-huh. — I have a big family. — Yeah, how many kids? — Me and two brothers, I'm the middle, and my mom and my dad and my grandmother. My grandmother passed away. This is a rare opportunity, where something happened years ago—

—and now we get to hear the other side of the story. Dave grew up in L.A. I grew up in L.A. I've seen Dave around at art shows and stuff. I've met you before — like, briefly, 'hey, what's up,' like that.
But we never got to hang out. I know you're a huge fan of— This is Bobby, by the way. — Nice to meet you. — Everyone, sorry for being rude. His L.A. street name: B-Triv.
That's Bobby Trivia. — I'm someone... KGB, is that what you were? Someone. So I've seen Dave in the art scene around. I know you like Kent Williams' art. — He's one of my favorite artists.

I love his shit. He's one of those rare artists that goes back and forth between fine art and comics. — Nice. So I had a show ten, fifteen years ago, at what was then Shepard Fairey and Dave Kinsey's Subliminal Projects in Los Angeles.
Nice. — And you're totally not going to remember this story. — I may. — Okay, but I may not. Every time I see Dave — this is the most normal I've ever seen you. — Oh, really? — Yeah.

Every time I see you — when I saw you at Sizzler, he was wearing a white violin jacket. — That's awesome. — But what's normal? — Okay, I don't know what normal is. — Yeah, I'm wearing a shirt of Bobby—
Bobby's face. — Look at your place. This place blew my mind. If this isn't normal, I don't want to be normal. It's my first art show — I think one of my first art shows in L.A.

Shepard Fairey was nice enough— — Where was it? — On Wilton and Wilshire, at Shepard Fairey's place. Absolutely. I stepped in midday. Yes, I stepped in midday. And since it's my first show in L.A., I'm excited.

You guys were just setting it up, though. — Okay, yeah. — Are you guys having pillow talk? — Yeah, there's some player talk. And— — Sorry to interrupt. — No, no, no. My family — the reason I mention my family is, I love my family.
Absolutely. But all they do is cause me pain. — Oh. Like, if I have an art show and I'm like, 'Mom, Dad, I just fucking sold out my show in London, I made millions of dollars—'
[mock father voice] 'Hey Dad, where's those paintings I had in the garage?' — 'Oh...' I gave them to the lady at the Korean mall, at the kiosk I go to. — I go, 'Dad, what the fuck are you doing?'

'I'm selling my shit for shit-tons of money now.' — 'Why are you yelling at me? Why are you yelling at me? She just sold them at the Antiques Roadshow. I'm hooking you up. She owns them all. She went on TV at the Antiques Roadshow.' — That's the game, though, isn't it?

What the fuck's money mean? It's all about art and love. 'I gave your paintings to the fucking Korean shopping mall.' — Yeah, but did whoever she gave it to figure it out? Did she make money? — And then, on the cheap paper, her family, her brothers and sisters, her little kids that have some money—

—to do their bucket shit, boom. That's the game. That's the game, players. — Yeah, right. I got something to eat, I go, 'Come on, take it. The way you help me is by not helping me. The way you help me is — I know they're trying—'

You help them, they help them — that's the game, player. You got your shit right. You need a jet. Listen, what I've noticed with people that have all the fucking money is: if they have all the money, shit just becomes more perfect. The more money you have, the more perfect everything is. Perfect.

People walking around, everything they're taking care of, every fucking thing. If you had the money, if you wanted, you could take a shit and have somebody come up and wipe your ass perfect. — Nice. — If you want that much money. Or, or — you could have your game going on, have all your shit—

—you want, you're fucking perfect, you're doing your thing, you have everything you need. All your people are taken care of, your family members are taken care of, everybody's comfortable. And then you got your shit going, and you can throw it out — throw more love. — Dave, the more money he has, the more problems.

See, that's the problem. — Is that the pleasure of having a lawyer? — The more money, the more problems. That's the problem. Because it ain't the problem. — That song is perfect for Dave. — All you need is enough money to be comfortable, and then you need to understand that money has no value.

When you have enough money, money has no value. The real value of money is love and kindness. So you can take that — like your father did — and give it to some people at the Korean mall, who may have passed that thing on, and then somebody was smart enough—

—to understand that that was your painting, held onto it, then sold it, and paid some of their bills, took care of some of their kids. You know what I mean? — This motherfucker's getting super deep now.

You need to have him come on, and he needs to talk to you. — No, yeah. — You want to get super deep? — Yeah, let's go deep. — Okay. I was going to save this for Bill Maher, but I'll share it with you.

Don't go, dude. — [announcer voice] News break! News break! News break! News break! — Explain the process of how the wealth gets thrown out. This is a new kindness game. — Yeah. I have a feeling that we're not playing this fucking game of life right.

That's my feeling. That's my personal feeling. I think we're all fucking full of shit. — Not really. — I think collectively we're actually fucking badasses, and full of kindness and love and heartfelt—
Like, we want to have fun, we want to do art. My whole goal is that we all create. — Right. — That's the only life. That's it. I love creating. — Yes. You do it, bro.

I walked into the fucking world — you're fucking doing it, player. You're doing it harder than me. You're doing it harder than me. And I walk in here and I'm like, okay, I just walked into my Disneyland.
You know what I mean? I love creating, I love making art — it's like happiness. I like practicing making babies. That's our only fucking thing. So the stupid thing is: we're getting cut—

The only thing we don't have is a fireball and a stripper pole. And, you know, whatever your creativity is — the judgment part. — Yeah, and talking about judging: me saying you look crazy every time I see you, I wasn't saying it as a bad thing. It's like, I get that a lot of people—

'This guy is going for it.' Listen — this is your world, right, player? I'm pointing my fingers from you to me. That's your world, right? That's your world. You make your own reality. And the thing is, I could go nuts, I could go out—

—with a fucking machine gun and take some people out and fuck up their worlds. I could play God on their worlds. And that's where the fucking game goes wrong. Hitler was really fucking good at the game.

He was. Call me a fucking asshole if you want to challenge me on this — but he was great at the game. He was so good at the game that he convinced fucking hundreds of thousands of people to kill a bunch of fucking people, because he was good at the game.

But he was playing the wrong game. — Right. Yes. So the game is creativity and love, and supporting, and fucking understanding — and money really has no value. The only value in money is love, and creativity, and encouraging others to do this shit.
So how do you get it? How do you get them to do that? I agree with you, by the way. — To get — okay, whatever your thoughts on Hitler are. — By the way, that's a drug.

Once we get this fucking creativity thing done— — Wait, wait, I'm trying to translate the sound. — Yes, we're all going to have them. — Wait, is it farting on them, or coming on them? — All of this stuff.

Little things like this become really fucking fun, and — we don't need fucking heroin anymore if we're all painting and doing silly things. — I'm with Dave. Whatever your thoughts on Hitler are, he convinced thousands, millions — I don't know — people to do something.

They're sheep, and he guided them toward a super evil, violent path. — Yeah. Had he done it the other way, and praised people and loved them, then he'd be like — Hitler with the long hair, like a hippie.

Well, I don't know if it's all about that. See, my thing is — whatever your world is, you know what I mean? My thing is this: we're all — this is your world, this is your world — we're all on the same playing field.
Right. Hitler's beliefs, whoever's fucking beliefs — that's their beliefs. That's their world. You know what I mean? They can choose to fucking kill Jews if they want—
Right. Which, in my world, is a really shitty, fucking asshole, horrible thing to do. — Right, yeah. — Or we can all join together and say: how are we collectively going to do what's cool?
Like, and fun — and allow people to do this. My thing is, you can't look up to people. You can't worship. You can respect people and love them, but you especially can't look down on people.

People walk around these fucking places — restaurant, whatever. — Dave. — Somebody's working back there, and they're like, 'Oh, they're serving me, I'm above them because they're serving me.' That's all bullshit. It's their world as much as it's mine.

But you're going super deep right now — for that? But how do we get them? What do you do when you're confronted by super negative, hateful shit? How do you get them over to what you're saying right now?
That's the hard part. — It is the hard part. — Dave's going super deep. — No, it's the hard part. But you know what my thing is? I try to keep it really fucking cool with everybody.

I try to be really respectful with everybody, ask people's names and try to remember them. Try to be honest and down. And if people are doing shit for me, I try to break them off when I can, take care of them, this and that.

You're spreading it around. — Yeah, but to me it's like — I don't know. — For you it's easy. — A lot of people are just shitheads. A lot of people are just shitheads — they wouldn't take the time to meet the dishwasher, the cook.
A lot of people are hurt. — Yeah. And their pain is fucking flipped over on its side. — So how do you heal? How do you heal? How do you heal the hurt? How do you heal the hurt?

Listen. Listen, yes. Violence is because you've been violated, right? The only reason you're violent is because you've been violated. You're innocent — you have all this love in your heart — but somebody's fucked with you.
So that love flips upside down, and it starts exploding. — How do you flip it back? — It's a synergistic effect. — How do you flip it back? — You flip it back by not taking it on.

Not holding it in your heart. Not fucking letting it kill you. — I can see you're very open in the way you think. You're very understanding. And obviously, to do these things you have to be cool and patient and all these things.

I lose my shit all the time — especially with the ones closest to me. I'm the biggest asshole to my girlfriend, you know what I mean? When she's right there. — That's normal. — She wakes me up, she wakes me up, and she starts hitting me with shit. I'm like, okay, listen — do you have no—

I say, listen — you have a baby, baby, listen. My mom was abused as a kid, and she used to wake some of us up slapping us with belts and shit. So when you hit me, it reminds me of that shit. Yeah. Give me some space.

We've got to understand — you understand? A BJ to wake up. A hand job. Oh yeah, if she gave me a BJ, right on, and then was like, 'Okay, listen, we have a few problems,' I'd be like, it's full, it's what I need. — She's playing the long game. She's playing along. She's like, 'Look, I want a very pleasant day.' — Wow. Absolutely.

It's gonna cost me a couple sucks. — You wake up in a great mood, and now you're ready. You're ready to do anything. She could do anything, anything — you're like, 'I'll do all this shit.' It's crazy, but it's true. Women — just give up three licks, you know? You're in a shitty mood, you're in a shitty mood, but that's where the fucking—

—silly game is, because we have all this morality and hypocrisy and individual beliefs. Sure, you might not think that's the right way to do it, but for me, that was the perfect solution. She could cool me out with something like that, whatever. — Guys, come up and hug and snuggle with me.

Super hug. — Before she hit me with all the problems. — Super cuddle. Super cuddle. Yes. Super hug. Super cuddle. Something sweet, gentle. Like a spork, not a spoon. — Yeah, exactly. A spork. A spork.

You're making it for guys too. Give it three licks. Give it three licks — a little titty, nice, whatever they want. A head scratch, a back scratch, whatever they're into. Something good. — Dave's getting super deep right now.
I need to go. — Sorry, I don't mean to get so deep. — No, no, no, I like it. — I had a spiritual experience. — I like it. What was your spiritual experience?

What happened? — Oh, I was in Las Vegas. — What happened? — You know I had a serious gambling problem. — Oh, you did? — Yeah, I went to rehab and everything for it. — No shit. — I almost lost all my money.
Oh shit, I'm so glad you dealt with that. — I had an angina episode in a casino. And I'm 37. — Fuck you. — And it sounds like 'vagina,' it's funny. — You're fucking— I love it.

What is it exactly? — It's like the beginning of a heart attack, your shit just — whatever. — So what happened to you in Vegas? Strip club? — No, I was on the one-girl hookers, little things — but I was walking back from a club, and the drunkest dude in the world was in front of me. He's just wobbling back and forth, like in a—
—fucking Buster Keaton, Charlie Chaplin, 'nobody's that drunk' kind of way, right? And you're just watching. And I was watching him, and it was like, boom — don't be like that. You know what I mean?

Right. So even though I drink a lot, and I got my issues, I was like, okay — don't be like that. Don't be like that guy. Don't be like that guy. — Yeah, but he was young too, and I'd probably been like that in my past.
So then I got past him, went through the casino, got in the elevator — and there was a kid there, an Asian kid, and I was like, 'Hey, how's your night?'

I know. — You guys got that shit? I mean, I got that shit too, I'm not saying — you know what I mean. — I hate Asians. I hate Asians. — But this kid was like, 'My life's been way better, Dave, way better since I started hanging out with the whites. White is right, they always tell me. It's a little bit better since—'

'—the whites entered my life.' So then I saw this kid in the elevator, and I was like, 'Hey, how's your night?' — You were being nice to him. — And he said, 'It fucking sucks, I just lost fifteen thousand dollars.' He was all caught up in it, right? I said, 'Oh man, I'm so sorry.' And then I went into the hotel room. My girl was—

—all sleepy, she went to bed, and I just went into, like, totally asking questions, hearing answers. — How come the weird shit always happens in Vegas? — Yeah, it always goes down like that, because — as crazy as it is, it's a bit of an epicenter for the whole of it.

So what happened? — It always goes down. Just little shit — like I was just talking to you about, seeing everything, everyone's equal — never look down, never look up. And this was recent. You see the worst of people and the best of people in Vegas.
You see guys that just win tons of money — 'Hey, it's on me!' You see guys that just lost fucking everything. You see the whole spectrum of human emotion in that city. — It's like a combo of you.
The bad combo. — It's like how you are right now, without women. — But I want to ask Dave this question, we got a little off track. So it's my first show, at Shepard Fairey's place in Los Angeles.
Shepard and Dave Kinsey's spot. And Dave walks in. And before — what I said about him dressing crazy, I wasn't saying that as a bad thing. I love it. Every time I see him, this guy's dressed crazy.
And I'm like, 'This guy doesn't give a fuck.' — Okay, I mean, you're wearing sweatshirts. — Yeah, I wear sweatpants every day, with pictures of my friends on my shirt. So I don't care either.

So when I see someone that's — you were dressed like the Riddler. You had a green suit with pinstripes. And I remember — why do I remember? Because of my fucking family. I don't like to invite my mom and dad to my shows.

You met my brother — specifically my brother Jimmy. My mom and dad come to my shows. They're born-again Christian, so they don't like a lot of the subject matter I paint. And they sort of do this blank denial — of looking at a naked chick and just pretending they didn't see it.

It's Eve. — Yeah, I'm like — [mock parent voice] they just see the vagina and go, 'It's a flower. Next. Oh, it's another flower. Next.' So my brother was there, and he was drunk, and I'm nervous, because I haven't had a lot of art shows, and I want to sell some paintings.

I want to make a living doing art. — You want to be rich. — I don't want to be rich, I want to make a living. And I see Dave, and I go, 'That's that fucking actor, he's in those movies, and he's dressed all crazy, and he looks like he might buy one of my paintings.'

Who comes in? My brother — drunk as shit. Jimmy Choe, my older brother. [drunk] 'Hey, hey, hey — you're fucking Dewey from Scream! You look like the Riddler from Batman, look at your suit, it's all green and stripes!' And you were so nice. I was like, 'Oh my God, shut the fuck up.' And you're like, 'Yeah, thanks, bro. Cool, cool.' It's like when people come up to me and go, 'Hey—'
'—you look like Steve Aoki,' and I go, 'Thanks. Thanks, man.' — 'Hey, you look like Steve Aoki.' And I go, 'Okay, cool, cool.' — Except he's Japanese and you're not. — He didn't let this shit go.
He was like, 'You look like the Riddler from Batman — the Adam West Batman.' And you were like, 'Thanks. That's a compliment.' — Yeah, but it was drunk-guy shit, and you never said, 'Fuck you, bro—'
'Get out of my face.' I was waiting for it, and it never — and you were like, 'Gotta go,' and you bounced. And I was like, oh my God. And I just wondered.

And he had his checkbook out. — Did you remember some Asian? It seems like you have annoying Asians. — No, it's really familiar. It was in the place above the Wiltern. — Yes, yes, exactly. — I remember a bike.

I remember seeing the original fucking thing there. And then I came back later. — Dave's a cool guy. He's awesome. — Best birthday I've ever been to. Amazing. He has his birthday at Sizzler. — I thought you had a good party at Sizzler.

And I go, 'Look.' — He had ballet, Dave! — I did this whole rant about how it's weird to make new friends as an adult, right? You have your homies as a kid, and then it's like — you meet people, or you know about people, and you're like, 'Oh, I respect them.'
And so it's a little strange, making new friends as an adult. I'm kind of making dope friends at this point in my life. I met some really fucking dope friends in the last, like, two years.

No joke — like real, deep fucking connection immediately. Like, oh shit — because sometimes you grow apart from the friends you grew up with. Yeah, and then you meet people later in life that you have more in common with. So we go to Sizzler, and it's bringing back all this shit, because you grew up eating Sizzler — we're doing, like, the—
—hugest commercial for Sizzler right now. — No, I'm saying, we are right now, I'm talking about it.

No, I mean — even doing the boarding show at Sizzler, those guys are — but you grew up on Sizzler. — I grew up on Sizzler, eating Sizzler cheese toast. I'm like, this is crazy. Dave's cool, and I'm walking out the door, and I see Pee-wee Herman just eating by himself at a table, and I'm like — I don't—

—want to be a dick, but you got to introduce me to Pee-wee Herman. I don't get starstruck — I don't — but I have to meet him. Dave has a painting in my room — they painted, like — well, I didn't see Sacha because it was from behind — but I'm like, 'Dave, I don't want to be the douchebag—'

'—you gotta introduce me to Pee-wee Herman.' He's like, 'Of course.' I sit down with Pee-wee — Paul Reubens — he's the fucking coolest dude. And then, when I sit down, I'm like, oh, fucking Borat's sitting across from me.
And then his wife sits down, and they're the coolest people ever. And I'm like — she's really a kid. — You didn't even know the other guy's Guy Oseary. Do you know Guy Oseary? — Guy Oseary?

Oh, it's amazing. — Oh yeah. I mean, I'm sure everyone's— — Madonna. He's fucking — he's Madonna's husband? — Manager. — Oh, manager. I'm sure everyone at this party knows somebody. He's also in on Uber.

Like, he's just a baller badass. — Oh, he's the Uber guy. — I went to his bar mitzvah. — Was that his wife? Was that his wife, the pregnant chick? — Yeah, beautiful. Was that amazing? — Michelle, she's awesome.
We're sitting with Pee-wee Herman, Sacha Baron Cohen, and this pregnant woman — beautiful pregnant woman — and she gets up, and her shit is all see-through. — I told you that. — It was so sick.
It was the most beautiful thing I've ever seen. — Yeah, because she's a dumbass model. — She's a beautiful girl. You could tell — being sexy even though she's pregnant. — You like that shit, Barney?
That's a guys' girl. — Yeah, I would have liked it. — You'd like to be pregnant? — No, I would have liked — I would like to be pregnant. — Bring that seahorse shit. Only a seahorse can be pregnant.

Male seahorse. Fuck yes, I'm down with that shit. — Fuck your foot, baby. — Dave, you're fucking awesome, though. — I know. It was such a great, great night. I can't wait. I'm sad we didn't go to Bootsy.

Yeah, you gotta shit it. We were wearing flip-flops, and you didn't want to— — It would have been really good. We had clothing issues, because— — No, I told you it would be good. I actually told the guy — Parker, the guy at the door—

I was like, 'Listen, David Choe's coming by. He might have flip-flops and shorts, but he's a dope-ass artist.' — I should have gone to your club, because instead I went to a roof party, where I met a black artist, Devin, and we got into this weird conversation — he's a black dude—
—that will not fuck black chicks, and only fucks Korean girls. And I'm like— — And I will — I'm out, I won't fuck Korean girls. I'm out. Yeah, I'm off the Koreans. No way. I've been to Itaewon.
Did I tell you that? — Why? — Yeah, you told me you went to — I've been to Korea. — Oh, because they give you a hard time or something? — Hey, don't take this the wrong way, okay?

And we're like, who's low-maintenance, no problems? — White girls. — You did white girls. — Oh, they don't know about that. — They're at the top of the food chain. — You fuck with Asians in the past. — Yeah, absolutely. — What, Koreans, Chinese? — Yeah. My homies, right, Kingsley and Third — that's, like, part of our home.

I'm talking about you. Have you had an Asian girlfriend? — Yeah — Korean, Japanese, Chinese, yes. And Japanese. You don't get very tight — but my brother went to Thailand, learned Thai, loves Thais, learned how to tie one on. You guys know what the red rope is? You don't know what the red rope is? Is that like—

—licorice? — That sounds good. — Oh, that's Red Vines. — Is it a certain time of the month? That's never happened before.
Wow, a girl just gave me a massage. A few girls just gave my entire body a massage with just their tongues — just their nipples. I'm like, 'Whoa, what? Can I have her number?'
And then a dude says to me, 'Why don't you get the red rope?' I go, 'I don't know what the red rope is. Why don't you tell me what the red rope is?'
What's the red rope? — It is phenomenal. We just found out about it tonight. It's not a place — it's a thing you can ask for. It's an experience. It's a phenomenal game.

It's a phenomenal game. — It's a red robe, god damn it. — Yeah, it's a red robe. — Wait, first of all, I gotta tell you this real quick. You know how it's okay for black people to call each other the N-word?
Yeah. They go, 'Hey, what's up,' and it's fine, because they're both black. — We're leaving Dodger Stadium right now. There's a car full of Asians wearing — how do you say it? Ryu—

Ryu. Ryu. They're wearing Ryu jerseys. They look at Critter, and they go, 'Fuck you, gook.' — That's not even that funny. — And everyone was — one had a Megan flag shirt on. First of all, that's not even the right term.
Yeah. And we were like, 'What?' — I just had my arm down the road. — Yeah, and I looked back at Dave. I figured they were talking to Dave. They looked right at Critter.
